name: Positive illusions
statement: Taylor and Brown argued that mildly inflated views of the self, of one's control and of one's future are normal and promote mental health.
meaning: Positive illusions is an umbrella term for three patterns treated as one syndrome: unrealistically positive self-evaluation, exaggerated perceptions of control, and unrealistic optimism. Whether each pattern exists is the subject of the entries on illusory superiority, illusion of control and optimism bias. This entry is about the further claim Taylor and Brown attached to them in 1988. That claim has two halves. The prevalence half says most healthy adults hold these beliefs, so accuracy cannot be a requirement of mental health. The adaptiveness half says the beliefs cause happiness, the ability to care about others and the capacity for productive work, rather than following from them. Only the second half is contested, and it is the half that made the paper famous.

origin.who: Shelley E. Taylor and Jonathon D. Brown
origin.note: The paper reviews existing work rather than reporting a study. Its target is the position, which it attributes to Jahoda and to Jourard and Landsman, that contact with reality is a criterion of mental health.

evidence: Taylor and Brown ran no experiment. They assembled evidence that most people hold overly positive self-evaluations, exaggerated perceptions of control or mastery, and unrealistic optimism, then asked whether those beliefs meet the criteria clinical writers use for mental health. Their method for the second step is stated openly. They take the criteria from Jahoda's 1958 review and from Jourard and Landsman, remove accurate self-perception from the list on the grounds that it is the thing in dispute, and keep three of what remains: happiness or contentment, the ability to care for and about others, and the capacity for creative and productive work. They then review studies linking each illusion to each criterion. Their own summary concedes that the research does not systematically address every illusion against every criterion and calls the evidence suggestive. Colvin and Block replied in 1994 that the logic and the studies failed to substantiate the thesis, and concluded that it remained unproven rather than false. Taylor and Brown's reply in the same issue narrowed the claim in three ways. The benefits are asserted for moderate illusion only, extreme illusion may be maladaptive, and illusion is not claimed to be necessary for mental health.

replication.headline: A meta-analysis of 299 samples puts self-enhancement at r = 0.18 with personal adjustment and at r = -0.01 with how other people rate the self-enhancer.
replication.detail: Dufner, Gebauer, Sedikides and Denissen pooled 299 samples and 126,916 people in 2019, defining self-enhancement as Taylor and Brown did. For self-reported personal adjustment the effect was r = .18, 95% CI [.17, .20], from 237 studies and 117,141 people. Self-enhancers reporting that they are happy is close to circular, so the informant analyses matter more. Informants rated self-enhancers as better adjusted, r = .12, 95% CI [.08, .17], k = 29, N = 4,760, and the six studies using trained mental health experts as raters gave r = .25, 95% CI [.17, .32], N = 681. Ten longitudinal studies covering 1,432 people found self-enhancement predicted later adjustment with concurrent correlations controlled, beta = .14, 95% CI [.09, .19]. Trim and fill filled 44 studies and moved the overall estimate to .14, 95% CI [.12, .16]. Under adverse life circumstances the effect was r = .16, 95% CI [.10, .21], k = 19, N = 3,440, which is the condition Taylor and Brown's cancer-patient work emphasised. The interpersonal side does not hold. Self-enhancement was unrelated to how favourably informants judged the person overall, r = -.01, 95% CI [-.06, .04], k = 55, N = 11,794. Split by acquaintance, it predicted approval from strangers, r = .11, 95% CI [.03, .18], k = 22, N = 3,633, and nothing from people who had met the target before, r = -.04, 95% CI [-.09, .01], k = 30, N = 7,201.

study.cite: Dufner, M., Gebauer, J. E., Sedikides, C., & Denissen, J. J. A. (2019). Self-enhancement and psychological adjustment: A meta-analytic review. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 23(1), 48-72.

limits: The measure is the weak point of the whole literature. Zuckerman and Knee pointed out in 1996 that a self-enhancement score built by subtracting others' ratings from self-ratings adds no variance once both ratings are in the model, so the index cannot show what self-enhancement does, and they proposed testing the interaction instead. Dufner and colleagues found that the objection has teeth in one specific case. Where self-enhancement was computed by subtracting informant ratings from self-ratings and correlated with an outcome also rated by informants, the result was negative for interpersonal adjustment, r = -.22, 95% CI [-.40, -.03], k = 8, N = 2,054, and for personal adjustment, r = -.17, 95% CI [-.26, -.08], k = 3, N = 437. That is the design of the best-known critical studies. Humberg and nine co-authors ran the sharpest test of the refined claim in 2019, using response surface analysis on five samples totalling 2,823 people and two ability domains. Most adjustment indicators were best predicted by how positive the self-view was, not by the gap between the self-view and measured ability, and the evidence went against both the self-knowledge hypothesis and the optimal margin hypothesis, which is the moderate-illusion position Taylor and Brown retreated to in 1994. One line of the argument has been tested on the body rather than on questionnaires. Taylor, Lerner, Sherman, Sage and McDowell put self-enhancers through a laboratory stress challenge in 2003 and found lower cardiovascular responses, faster recovery and lower baseline cortisol, against the view that self-enhancement is defensive neuroticism carrying a physiological cost. Dufner's interpersonal measures record how informants rate the target, which is not the same as Taylor and Brown's criterion of the ability to care for and about others, and no pooled test of that criterion was located. The full text of Colvin and Block 1994 sits behind a paywall; the account of its argument here comes from its published abstract and from Taylor and Brown's reply, which is an interested source.
misreadings: The 1988 paper is a literature review. Figures attributed to it belong to the studies it cites, and it reports no effect of its own. Taylor and Brown do not claim that illusion is necessary for mental health, that more illusion is better, or that illusions cure disease, and they say all three in print in 1994. Depressive realism is often presented as the evidence the thesis rests on; Taylor and Brown say their argument does not depend on it, and it did not survive replication in any case. The finding is also flattened in both directions. Colvin and Block did not show that illusions damage mental health, only that the case for benefit was unproven, and Dufner's meta-analysis does not vindicate the whole formulation, because the personal half comes out positive and the interpersonal half comes out at zero. Robins and Beer add a timing qualification. Students who overrated their academic ability on entry showed falling self-esteem and well-being and growing disengagement over college, with no gain in grades or graduation rates.
